idiom_name: sealed interface + records per rule + pattern-matching switch (exhaustive, no default arm)
implementation_notes: Modern Java: a sealed interface plus one record per grammar rule, and one switch over the sealed type that deconstructs records. From Java 21 (JEP 441) the switch is exhaustive without a default arm, so adding a node breaks every evaluator at compile time; that exhaustiveness is the point, which is why this variant's floor is Java 21 - on Java 17 the same shape compiles with pattern matching for instanceof plus a default arm that throws, which gives up the guarantee. Records remove the boilerplate of the classic hierarchy, so the sealed form is the default and the class-per-rule form is reserved for grammars that third parties must extend.
pitfalls: Sealing confines the hierarchy to one module (and, for classes, one package): a grammar that consumers must extend cannot be sealed.
Records are shallowly immutable - an array or list component stays mutable - so a node's children can change under a caller that assumed value semantics.
Recursion depth is the limit for deep expressions; there is no tail-call elimination, so bound input depth before evaluating untrusted text.
On Java 17 pattern matching for switch is not final: the same source needs a default arm, which silently swallows the next new node.

variants.name: Abstract Expression class with interpret(Context) per node
variants.idiom_name: abstract class Expression + one subclass per grammar rule implementing interpret(Context)
variants.implementation_notes: The GoF shape as the book writes it: an abstract Expression declaring interpret(Context) and a concrete class per grammar rule. It runs on any Java version, keeps the hierarchy open for extension by subclassing, and puts each rule's semantics in its own file; in exchange a new operation means editing every node class, and nothing proves the node set is complete. Choose it for libraries that expose the grammar to third-party node authors, and pair it with a visitor once several operations must walk the same tree.
pitfalls: Every rule is a separately loaded class: a real grammar becomes dozens or hundreds of files with class-loading and cold-start costs.
Adding an operation (print, optimise, type-check) means touching all node classes unless a visitor or an external switch is introduced - the expression problem in its classic form.
The hierarchy is open, so the node set can grow without any evaluator noticing; keep the hierarchy closed by convention (final classes, package-private constructors).
